name: polyguard
description: Multilingual prompt-injection scanner. Tests whether a chatbot's guardrails hold up in languages other than English, with the statistics to back the claim.

paragraphs: Live: (scans there are simulated until an API key is configured)

In three sentences. A chatbot that refuses a trick in English can fall for the same trick in Hindi, Swahili or Tagalog, and the people who meet that weaker chatbot are the ones least served by English-only testing. PolyGuard sends the same attacks to a chatbot in 73 languages, checks that the chatbot understood each language at all, and tests whether some languages are really less protected rather than unlucky. Then it writes defence rules and measures, against a placebo, how much they help on attacks it held back.

Most AI safety testing happens in English. PolyGuard takes a chatbot's system prompt, attacks a live copy of that bot with 5 kinds of prompt injection in every language in its attack bank, and shows, per language and per resource tier, which attacks got through. The point is to measure the gap between how well a bot is defended in English and how well it is defended in everyone else's language. The people that gap leaves exposed are the ones least served by English-only testing: patients, students and families who use a clinic's, a school's or a bank's chatbot in the language they speak at…

requirements.text: They need an API key or native speakers, so they do not exist yet.

A live scan needs all of: a key, a configured passcode (no passcode means no live scans, never open access), the passcode in the request, and room in a spend guard shared by every server instance through Supabase: a daily budget of paid calls, a per-visitor hourly limit, and a cap on scans running at once.
